edges.effect_quant: In the 2014 Nature study, 4 of 7 healthy volunteers developed a poorer glycemic response after 6 to 7 days of saccharin at the acceptable daily intake; however, a later double-blind parallel-arm study using pure saccharin at the maximum acceptable daily intake for 2 weeks in 46 healthy adults found no change in OGTT glucose or hormonal responses.
edges.population: healthy adults or adults at metabolic risk exposed to short-term saccharin or mixed artificial-sweetener challenges
edges.mechanism: Saccharin may affect glucose tolerance through microbiome-dependent changes in fermentation and host signaling or through intestinal sweet-taste receptor pathways, but human responses appear heterogeneous and highly context dependent.
edges.summary: Saccharin has one of the more concerning mechanistic sweetener signals because small interventional work suggests some people can develop worse glycemic responses after brief exposure. At the same time, a larger pure-saccharin randomized trial was negative, so the overall edge is best read as early harmful evidence rather than settled metabolic toxicity.
edges.caveats: This literature is small, protocol-sensitive, and partly driven by responder subgroups. Commercial formulations, background diet, habitual sweetener use, and microbiome composition likely matter a great deal, and one mixed-sweetener pilot found no acute blood glucose effect at all.

evidence.notes: Artificial sweeteners induce glucose intolerance by altering the gut microbiota.
